chapter: Moten band, Kansas City and the evolution of jazz
title: Harmony from added sixths to the bebop 11ths, and why it was cut off
summary: He traces how McKinney's Cotton Pickers and Don Redman added sixths, then ninths and 11ths, and bebop used the whole scale until the business turned back to triads in the 1940s.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: chords to utilizing the whole scale in your playing. And harmonization. Where before we played just three part harmony. Along about 1928 McKinney's Cotton Pickers came in adding the sixth. And this was an evolution. In fact, when I added the sixth to our chords out there in Minneapolis, the leader wouldn't play those arrangements because he said they sounded bad. And McKinney's Cotton Pickers started this and when Don Redman came in they started using five brass and six, you know, like that. So it got even Paul Whiteman's band in the twenties, he had a big band but they never bothered with anything more than three part harmony.

Yeah, that's right. But now -- because that was the classical sound. But guys like John Nesbit and Don Redman started this, adding the sixth and then everybody started doing it. And they started using more pieces. Then they started adding the ninth and all of that and the 13th and 11th and everything in the chords.

So then the boppers did that, started using the augmented 11th. So finally they were using the whole scale. And they still haven't finished yet but someone cut the whole thing off around the 1940's. In the forties they cut the whole thing off and went back to the beginning again with the triads and church harmony with the rock. And a lot of the

rhythm and blues stuff.
So the people that controlled the business stopped us. Because we can still go farther yet with harmony and everything. And as I say, the people, ordinary names here, it gets a little bit complicated unless there are people that really follow music, you know. When you start listening to more than three horns and things, you just start to get so involved that you can't keep it all together. So that's why today most of the people are interested mostly in solos, you know.
